concepts.title: Weißt du noch? 'Do you remember?'
concepts.explanation: Adding noch to wissen turns 'know' into 'still know', which is how Germans say 'remember' in conversation. Weißt du noch, als ...? means 'Do you remember when ...?'. A simple Weißt du das noch? means 'Do you remember that?'

examples.text: Weißt du noch, als wir in Rom waren?
examples.en: Do you remember when we were in Rome?

examples.text: Weißt du noch, wo das Haus war?
examples.en: Do you remember where the house was?

concepts.title: warten auf: 'to wait for'
concepts.explanation: German says 'wait on' instead of 'wait for': warten auf + accusative. Don't use für here. Wir warten auf dich means 'We're waiting for you.'

examples.text: Die Kinder warten auf ihre Mutter.
examples.en: The children are waiting for their mother.

concepts.title: auf dem Land: 'in the countryside'
concepts.explanation: Land means 'country' (a nation), but auf dem Land means 'in the countryside', as opposed to the city. Compare: Er kommt aus einem anderen Land (another country) and Sie lebt auf dem Land (she lives in the country).

examples.text: Meine Eltern leben auf dem Land.
examples.en: My parents live in the countryside.

examples.text: Ich will nicht auf dem Land leben.
examples.en: I don't want to live in the country.

examples.text: Als Kind war ich oft auf dem Land.
examples.en: As a child I was often in the countryside.

concepts.title: Wie alt bist du? Talking about age
concepts.explanation: German asks age with wie alt ('how old') plus sein: Wie alt bist du? The answer uses sein too, often with Jahre alt: Ich bin drei Jahre alt. Never use haben for age.

examples.text: Das Kind ist drei Jahre alt.
examples.en: The child is three years old.

concepts.title: sie and ihnen: 'they' and 'them'
concepts.explanation: Plural sie means 'they' as the subject and also 'them' as a direct object. After dative words like mit, bei, helfen or gehören it becomes ihnen: mit ihnen = 'with them'. Lowercase ihnen is 'them'; capitalized Ihnen is formal 'you'.

examples.en: I want to talk to them.

concepts.title: fahren vs. gehen: how you go
concepts.explanation: gehen means going on foot (or going in general), while fahren means going by car, train, bike or any vehicle. So a trip to another city is usually fahren: Wir fahren nach Berlin. Auto fahren means 'to drive'.

concepts.title: genug: before nouns, after adjectives
concepts.explanation: genug ('enough') usually comes before a noun, just like in English: genug Geld. But with an adjective it comes after it: alt genug, gut genug. It never takes an ending.

concepts.title: welcher / welche / welches: 'which'
concepts.explanation: welch- means 'which' or 'what' when choosing from options. It takes the same endings as der/die/das: welcher (masc.), welche (fem. and plural), welches (neuter). Like other question words, it sends the verb to the end in a sub-clause: Ich weiß nicht, welche Tür es ist.

examples.text: Welche Sprache spricht man in Wien?
examples.en: What language do they speak in Vienna?

concepts.notes: generated by claude-opus-5-5 (tools/generate.py, 2026-11-28) | REVIEW warning: welch- takes the same endings as dieser, not der/die/das (the neuter article is das, not -es); suggest 'the same endings as dieser/diese/dieses'.

concepts.title: welche: 'some' standing alone
concepts.explanation: In everyday speech welche on its own can mean 'some' or 'any', replacing a plural noun already mentioned. Kinder? Sie haben welche. = 'Children? They have some.' English often just says 'some' or 'one'.

examples.text: Wir haben keine Kinder, aber sie haben welche.
examples.en: We don't have any children, but they have some.

examples.text: Es gibt welche, die das nicht wissen.
examples.en: There are some who don't know that.

concepts.notes: generated by claude-opus-5-5 (tools/generate.py, 2026-11-28) | REVIEW warning: 'English often just says some or one' is misleading, because plural welche never corresponds to 'one'; suggest 'some' or 'any' (e.g. 'Do you have any?').

concepts.title: The perfect tense with sein
concepts.explanation: Most verbs form the perfect with haben, but some use sein instead: verbs of movement or change of state, and passieren ('to happen'). So 'What happened?' is Was ist passiert?, not 'hat passiert'. The participle still goes to the end.

concepts.title: erst: 'only', 'not until', 'first'
concepts.explanation: With times and ages, erst means 'only' in the sense of 'no later/more than that so far' or 'not until': Er kommt erst morgen = He's not coming until tomorrow. Use nur for plain amounts and limits, erst when time is involved. erst can also mean 'first', before something else: Ich muss erst nach Hause = I have to go home first.

examples.en: I have to go home first.

concepts.title: dar- before a vowel: darüber, daran
concepts.explanation: When the preposition in a da- word starts with a vowel, German adds an r: da + über = darüber, da + an = daran (but davon, damit). These words mean 'about it', 'of it' and so on, and refer to things or ideas. For people, use the preposition with a pronoun: über ihn = about him.

examples.en: I don't know anything about it.

concepts.title: bekommen means 'get', not 'become'
concepts.explanation: bekommen looks like English 'become', but it means 'to get, to receive': Wir bekommen Geld = We get money. 'To become' in German is werden. Its past participle has no ge-: Ich habe es bekommen = I got it.

examples.review: Same issue as the entry sentence: 'Er hat die Arbeit bekommen' = 'He got the job' is not quite idiomatic; consider a different example such as 'Ich habe nie Geld von ihm bekommen.'

concepts.title: darf: 'may', 'be allowed to'
concepts.explanation: darf (from dürfen) is the modal verb for permission: Darf ich? = May I? Like other modals, the second verb goes to the end as an infinitive. darf nicht means 'must not, not allowed' – don't mix it up with muss nicht, which means 'don't have to'.

examples.en: You're not allowed to eat here.
Nobody can find out about this.

concepts.title: dies: 'this' standing alone
concepts.explanation: dies is a short form of dieses, used on its own, mostly with sein: Dies ist mein Zimmer = This is my room. It never changes, whatever noun follows. It sounds a bit formal; in everyday speech das is more common: Das ist mein Zimmer.

concepts.title: hören auf: 'to listen to', 'to obey'
concepts.explanation: hören on its own means 'to hear'. To say you listen to a person (take their advice, obey them), German uses hören auf + accusative: Die Kinder hören nicht auf mich = 'The kids don't listen to me.'

examples.text: Die Kinder hören nicht auf mich.
examples.en: The kids don't listen to me.

examples.text: Kinder müssen auf ihre Eltern hören.
examples.en: Children have to listen to their parents.

concepts.title: auf dem Weg: 'on the way'
concepts.explanation: 'On my way' is auf dem Weg, literally 'on the way'. German doesn't say 'my' here. Add a destination with nach or zu: auf dem Weg nach Hause = 'on the way home'.

examples.text: Wir sind schon auf dem Weg nach Hause.
examples.en: We're already on our way home.

examples.text: Auf dem Weg zur Arbeit habe ich ihn gesehen.
examples.en: I saw him on the way to work.

concepts.title: ganze: 'the whole', 'all the'
concepts.explanation: Before a noun, ganz means 'whole' or 'entire' and takes an adjective ending: die ganze Zeit = 'the whole time'. It often translates as 'all': das ganze Geld = 'all the money', die ganze Nacht = 'all night'.

examples.text: Ich war die ganze Zeit hier.
examples.en: I was here the whole time.
The whole house belongs to him.

concepts.title: Mal vs. Zeit: two kinds of 'time'
concepts.explanation: English 'time' has two German words. Zeit is time as an amount (Ich habe keine Zeit = 'I have no time'). Das Mal is one occasion: dieses Mal = 'this time', das eine Mal = 'that one time'. Don't confuse the noun Mal with the little softening word mal.

concepts.title: After der/die/das: adjective ends in -e or -en
concepts.explanation: After der, die, das (and dieser), an adjective before a noun ends in either -e or -en. It's -e in the basic forms: die ganze Stadt, das ganze Haus. Almost everywhere else it's -en: den ganzen Tag, im ganzen Haus, in der ganzen Welt, die ganzen Leute.

examples.text: Ich war den ganzen Tag zu Hause.
examples.en: I was at home all day.
The whole town is talking about it.
There's nobody in the whole house.

concepts.notes: generated by claude-opus-5-5 (tools/generate.py, 2026-11-28) | REVIEW warning: 'It's -e in the basic forms' is vague; say that -e is used in the nominative singular (der ganze Tag, die ganze Stadt, das ganze Haus) and the feminine/neuter accusative singular, and -en everywhere else.

concepts.title: dachte: a past with -te and a vowel change
concepts.explanation: A few verbs mix both past patterns: they add -te like regular verbs and also change their stem. denken (to think) becomes dachte: Ich dachte, du bist in Berlin = 'I thought you were in Berlin.' Learn these few forms as you meet them.

examples.en: I thought this would be easy.
She was thinking of her brother.

concepts.title: Liebe ...: 'Dear ...' in greetings
concepts.explanation: To start a letter or message, German uses the adjective lieb ('dear'). Before a woman's name or a plural it's Liebe (Liebe Ann, Liebe Freunde); before a man's name it's Lieber (Lieber David). Don't confuse it with the noun die Liebe, 'love'.

examples.text: Liebe Ann, wie geht es dir?
Liebe Freunde, das ist mein Bruder Sami.
examples.en: Dear friends, this is my brother Sami.

examples.text: Liebe Kinder, jetzt gehen wir nach Hause.
examples.en: Dear children, now we're going home.

concepts.title: scheinen + zu: 'to seem to'
concepts.explanation: scheinen means 'to seem'. Like English, it is followed by zu + infinitive, which goes to the end: Er scheint alles zu wissen ('He seems to know everything'). You can also say Es scheint, dass ... ('It seems that ...').

examples.text: Es scheint, dass er nicht kommt.

concepts.title: wäre + past participle: 'would have (come)'
concepts.explanation: Verbs that form the perfect with sein (like kommen) use wäre instead of hätte for 'would have done'. The participle goes to the end: Ich wäre gerne gekommen ('I would have liked to come').

examples.en: I would have liked to come.

examples.text: Ohne dich wäre ich nicht gekommen.
examples.en: Without you I wouldn't have come.

examples.text: Er wäre gekommen, aber er hatte keine Zeit.
examples.en: He would have come, but he didn't have time.

concepts.title: dafür sein: 'to be in favor'
concepts.explanation: Ich bin dafür literally means 'I am for it' and is the normal way to say 'I'm in favor'. Ich bin nicht dafür means 'I'm against it'.

examples.text: Mein Vater ist dafür, meine Mutter nicht.
examples.en: My father is for it, my mother isn't.

concepts.title: dafür: 'but then, to make up for it'
concepts.explanation: After mentioning a downside, dafür introduces something good that balances it out, like English 'but then' or 'on the other hand'. It often comes right after aber: Das Haus ist alt, aber dafür sehr schön.

examples.text: Das Haus ist alt, aber dafür sehr schön.
examples.en: The house is old, but very beautiful to make up for it.

examples.text: Er spricht kein Französisch, dafür aber sehr gut Englisch.
examples.en: He doesn't speak French, but then he speaks very good English.

examples.text: Die Arbeit ist schwer, aber dafür gibt es viel Geld.
examples.en: The work is hard, but then it pays a lot.

concepts.title: gleich: 'in a moment' and 'the same'
concepts.explanation: As a time word, gleich means 'right away' or 'in a moment': Ich bin gleich da. As an adjective it means 'the same' or 'equal': Wir sind gleich alt ('We're the same age'). Das ist mir gleich means 'I don't care'.

concepts.title: zwischen: 'between'
concepts.explanation: zwischen means 'between' or 'among'. When it says where something is, it takes the dative: zwischen mir und meinem Bruder, zwischen mir und der Tür.

examples.text: Er steht zwischen mir und der Tür.
examples.en: He's standing between me and the door.

examples.text: Ich bin zwischen zwei und drei Uhr zu Hause.
examples.en: I'm at home between two and three o'clock.

concepts.title: je: 'ever' and 'each'
concepts.explanation: In questions and negative sentences, je means 'ever': Hast du je so etwas gesehen? Before a number or ein it means 'each': Die Kinder bekommen je ein Buch ('one book each').

examples.text: Hast du je so etwas gesehen?
examples.en: Have you ever seen anything like it?

examples.text: Die Kinder bekommen je ein Buch.
examples.en: The children get one book each.

concepts.title: Es kommt darauf an: 'it depends'
concepts.explanation: Es kommt darauf an is the everyday way to say 'it depends'. To say what it depends on, add a clause with the verb at the end: Es kommt darauf an, was du willst ('It depends on what you want').

examples.text: Es kommt darauf an, was du willst.
examples.en: It depends on what you want.

examples.text: Es kommt darauf an, wann er kommt.
examples.en: It depends on when he comes.

concepts.title: nicht brauchen zu: 'don't need to'
concepts.explanation: brauchen means 'to need'. With nicht (or kein, nichts, nur) plus zu + infinitive it means 'don't need to', just like muss nicht: Er braucht nicht zu kommen ('He doesn't need to come'). The infinitive with zu goes to the end.

examples.text: Ihr braucht keine Angst zu haben.
examples.en: You don't need to be afraid.

concepts.title: ein paar: 'a few'
concepts.explanation: ein paar means 'a few' or 'a couple of'. It is written lowercase and never changes its ending, whatever the case: ein paar Freunde, mit ein paar Freunden. The noun after it is plural.

examples.text: Ich habe ein paar Freunde in Berlin.
examples.en: I have a few friends in Berlin.

examples.text: Ein paar Leute sind noch hier.
examples.en: A few people are still here.

examples.text: Er hat ein paar Fehler gemacht.

concepts.title: ist gewesen: the perfect of sein
concepts.explanation: The verb sein forms its perfect tense with sein itself plus the participle gewesen: ich bin gewesen, du bist gewesen. It means 'have been' or simply 'was'. In everyday speech war is more common, but gewesen is used a lot in questions like Wo bist du gewesen?

examples.text: Ich bin noch nie in Rom gewesen.

concepts.title: am Ende vs. zu Ende
concepts.explanation: am Ende means 'in the end' or 'at the end': Am Ende war alles gut. zu Ende with sein means 'over, finished': Die Schule ist zu Ende (school is over).

examples.en: In the end, everything was fine.

examples.text: Es ist noch nicht zu Ende.

concepts.title: liegen: 'to lie', 'to be (lying)'
concepts.explanation: German often says where things are with position verbs instead of sein. liegen is used for things lying flat (a book, a dog on the floor), stehen for things standing upright. Das Buch liegt im Auto = The book is in the car.

examples.en: The book is in the car.

examples.text: Der Hund liegt vor der Tür.
examples.en: The dog is lying in front of the door.

concepts.title: liegen an: 'to be because of', 'to be up to'
concepts.explanation: Es liegt an ... + dative says what or who is the cause of something, or whose decision it is. Es liegt an dir = It's up to you / It's because of you. With a whole clause, use daran, dass ...

concepts.title: während: 'during'
concepts.explanation: As a preposition, während means 'during'. It takes the genitive, so feminine nouns use der: während der Woche (during the week). In casual speech you may also hear it with the dative.

examples.text: Während der Woche bin ich in Berlin.
examples.en: During the week I'm in Berlin.

examples.text: Während der Arbeit hat er keine Zeit.
examples.en: He has no time during work.

examples.text: Während dieser Zeit war ich in Rom.
examples.en: During that time I was in Rome.

concepts.title: während: 'while' (verb at the end)
concepts.explanation: während can also join two clauses, meaning 'while' (at the same time) or 'whereas' (contrast). Like dass and weil, it sends the verb to the end of its clause: ..., während er spricht.

examples.text: Marie sagt nichts, während er spricht.
examples.en: Marie says nothing while he's talking.

examples.text: Während wir warten, können wir etwas essen.
examples.en: While we wait, we can eat something.

examples.text: Er hat viel Geld, während ich nichts habe.
examples.en: He has a lot of money, whereas I have nothing.

concepts.title: reden vs. sprechen
concepts.explanation: Both mean 'to talk'. reden is very common in everyday conversation (Wir müssen reden), while sprechen is a bit more neutral and is the verb for speaking a language: Er spricht Französisch. With people, both use mit and über.
concepts.notes: generated by claude-opus-5-5 (tools/generate.py, 2026-11-28) | REVIEW warning: 'With people, both use mit and über' is confusing, because über introduces the topic, not the person. Suggest 'Both use mit for the person (mit dir reden) and über for the topic (über Geld reden)'.

concepts.title: früher: 'used to', 'in the past'
concepts.explanation: German has no word for 'used to'. Instead, put früher ('in the past') with a past-tense verb: Früher hatte ich einen Hund = I used to have a dog. Früher can also simply mean 'earlier': Kannst du früher kommen?

examples.en: I used to have a dog.

concepts.title: gefallen: 'to like' turned around
concepts.explanation: With gefallen, the thing you like is the subject and the person who likes it is in the dative. Das gefällt mir literally means 'that pleases me', i.e. 'I like that'. Use it for things you see or experience; for food and general liking, mögen is also common.

concepts.title: lieber: 'rather', 'prefer'
concepts.explanation: lieber is the comparative of gern: gern = 'like to', lieber = 'prefer to, would rather'. Add it to a verb to show preference: Ich gehe lieber allein = I'd rather go alone. With sollte it gives advice: Sie sollten lieber gehen = You'd better go.

examples.review: The translation 'Water, please.' hides the 'rather/prefer' meaning that this concept example is meant to teach. Suggest '– I'd rather have water.'

concepts.title: Ich hoffe es / Ich hoffe nicht
concepts.explanation: English says 'I hope so', but German uses es instead of 'so': Ich hoffe es. 'I hope not' is simply Ich hoffe nicht. To say what you hope, add a dass clause or just a normal sentence after a comma: Ich hoffe, er kommt bald.

concepts.title: heißen: 'to be called'
concepts.explanation: German asks for names with heißen ('to be called'): Wie heißt du? = What's your name? (literally 'How are you called?'). Note it's wie ('how'), not was ('what'). The answer works the same way: Sie heißt Jane = Her name is Jane.

concepts.title: heißen: 'to mean'; das heißt
concepts.explanation: heißen also means 'to mean': Was heißt das? = What does that mean? Das heißt ... ('that means', written d. h.) is used like English 'that is' or 'i.e.' to explain something. Es heißt, ... means 'they say, it is said'.

examples.text: Das heißt, wir haben keine Zeit mehr.
examples.en: That means we don't have any time left.

concepts.title: Countries: usually no article
concepts.explanation: Most country names are neuter and are used without der/die/das, just like city names. Use in for being there, nach for going there, and aus for coming from there: Ich bin in Australien, Ich gehe nach Australien, Ich komme aus Australien.

concepts.title: Meiner Meinung nach: 'in my opinion'
concepts.explanation: To say 'in my opinion', German uses meiner Meinung nach, with nach placed after the noun. Since this phrase fills the first position, the verb comes right after it: Meiner Meinung nach ist das gut.

examples.text: Meiner Meinung nach ist das ein Fehler.
examples.en: In my opinion, that's a mistake.

examples.text: Meiner Meinung nach ist das nicht wahr.
examples.en: In my opinion, that isn't true.

examples.text: Meiner Meinung nach kommt er nicht.
examples.en: In my opinion, he won't come.

concepts.title: überhaupt: 'at all' and 'anyway'
concepts.explanation: With nicht, kein or nichts, überhaupt strengthens the negative like 'at all': überhaupt nicht = not at all. In questions it means 'anyway' or 'even' and often sounds a bit impatient: Was willst du überhaupt?

examples.en: I have no time at all.

concepts.title: lang vs. lange
concepts.explanation: lang is the adjective 'long' and describes things: Der Weg ist lang. lange is the adverb 'for a long time' and describes how long something goes on: Ich bin schon lange hier. Don't mix them up: 'a long time' is always lange.

concepts.title: Time + lang: 'for' a period
concepts.explanation: To say how long something lasted, put lang after a time expression in the accusative: eine Woche lang = for a week. It's like English 'all day long', but works with any span of time: zwei Jahre lang.

examples.text: Wir waren eine Woche lang in Rom.
examples.en: We were in Rome for a week.

examples.text: Tony war zwei Jahre lang in Wien.
examples.en: Tony was in Vienna for two years.

examples.text: Er hat den ganzen Tag lang nichts gesagt.
examples.en: He didn't say anything all day long.

concepts.title: morgen vs. der Morgen
concepts.explanation: Lowercase morgen is an adverb meaning 'tomorrow'. Capitalized der Morgen is a noun meaning 'morning'. You see the noun in time phrases like heute Morgen ('this morning'), am Morgen ('in the morning') and jeden Morgen ('every morning').

examples.text: Heute Morgen war ich in der Stadt.
examples.en: This morning I was in town.

examples.text: Am Morgen habe ich keine Zeit.
examples.en: I don't have time in the morning.

concepts.title: Wie spät ist es? Asking the time
concepts.explanation: To ask the time, Germans literally say 'How late is it?': Wie spät ist es? The answer uses Uhr, as in Es ist drei Uhr.

examples.text: Weißt du, wie spät es ist?
examples.en: Do you know what time it is?

concepts.title: zu spät kommen: 'to be late'
concepts.explanation: When someone arrives late, German says zu spät ('too late'), not just spät. Er kommt zu spät means 'He's late', even though the words say 'too late'. On its own, Es ist zu spät still means 'It's too late'.

examples.text: Bob kam heute Morgen zu spät.

concepts.title: The perfect passive: ist ... worden
concepts.explanation: To say something 'has been done', use ist + past participle + worden: Das ist gesagt worden ('That has been said'). In the passive, the participle of werden is worden, without ge-. The form geworden is only used for 'become': Er ist alt geworden.

examples.text: Das Geld ist nie gefunden worden.

concepts.title: Ich bin deiner Meinung: 'I agree'
concepts.explanation: To agree with someone, say you are 'of their opinion', using the genitive: Ich bin deiner Meinung ('I agree with you'). Ich bin auch dieser Meinung means 'I think so too', and Wir sind einer Meinung means 'We agree'.

concepts.title: weg: 'away, gone'
concepts.explanation: Lowercase weg is an adverb meaning 'away' or 'gone', very often with sein: Er ist weg (He's gone). With a modal verb it can mean 'leave': Ich muss jetzt weg (I have to go now). Don't confuse it with the noun der Weg (the way, the path), which is capitalized.

concepts.title: recht haben: 'to be right'
concepts.explanation: German says 'to have right' instead of 'to be right': Du hast recht (You're right). Use haben, not sein. You may also see it written with a capital: Recht haben.

concepts.title: Ist dir das recht? 'Is that OK with you?'
concepts.explanation: With sein and a dative person, recht means 'all right, acceptable': Das ist mir recht (That's fine with me). The person who agrees is in the dative (mir, dir, Ihnen), just like with gefallen.

examples.en: Is that all right with you?

concepts.title: dabei: 'there', 'on you', 'with it'
concepts.explanation: dabei sein means 'to be there, to take part': Ich war dabei (I was there). Etwas dabei haben means 'to have something on you': Hast du Geld dabei? It can also mean 'with it, in doing so': Kannst du mir dabei helfen?

examples.en: Do you have money on you?

concepts.title: dabei: 'and yet', 'even though'
concepts.explanation: dabei can add a surprising contrast: Er hat keine Zeit, dabei hat er nichts zu tun (He has no time, and yet he has nothing to do). dabei fills the first position, so the verb comes right after it, not at the end.

examples.text: Er hat keine Zeit, dabei hat er nichts zu tun.
examples.en: He has no time, and yet he has nothing to do.

examples.text: Er spricht kein Französisch, dabei war er drei Jahre in Paris.
examples.en: He doesn't speak French, even though he was in Paris for three years.

examples.text: Sie ist allein, dabei hat sie eine große Familie.
examples.en: She's alone, even though she has a big family.

concepts.title: die Hand, not 'my hand': articles with body parts
concepts.explanation: With body parts German often uses der/die/das where English uses 'my, your, his'. Was hast du in der Hand? means 'What do you have in your hand?'. The person is often shown with a dative pronoun: Er gab mir die Hand (He shook my hand).

examples.text: Was hast du in der Hand?
examples.en: What do you have in your hand?

concepts.title: The past perfect: hatte + past participle
concepts.explanation: To say something had already happened before another past event, use hatte/hatten (or war/waren for sein-verbs) plus the past participle at the end. It works just like the perfect tense, only with the past form of the helper verb: Wir hatten das schon gemacht = We had already done that.

examples.text: Als Thomas kam, hatten wir schon alles gemacht.
examples.en: When Thomas came, we had already done everything.

concepts.title: wegen: 'because of'
concepts.explanation: wegen means 'because of' and is followed by a noun, not a whole clause (for a clause, use weil). In careful German it takes the genitive: wegen der Arbeit = because of work. In everyday speech you also hear it with pronouns like wegen dir = because of you.

examples.text: Ich bin wegen der Arbeit hier.
Wegen der Kinder bleiben wir zu Hause.
examples.en: Because of the children, we're staying home.

examples.text: Ich bin nur wegen dir gekommen.
examples.en: I only came because of you.

Suggest adding a short clause that colloquial wegen often takes the dative, as in 'wegen dir'.

concepts.title: Glück haben and zum Glück
concepts.explanation: German says 'to have luck' where English says 'to be lucky': Du hast Glück = You're lucky. zum Glück means 'luckily, fortunately', and Viel Glück! means 'Good luck!'. Glück can also mean 'happiness'.

concepts.title: Jobs without 'a': Er ist Lehrer
concepts.explanation: When you say what someone's job is, German uses no article: Mein Vater ist Lehrer = My father is a teacher. The same goes after werden: Er will Lehrer werden. For a woman, the job word usually gets -in: Lehrerin.

examples.en: He wants to become a teacher.
Ken is a teacher in Vienna.

concepts.title: Genau!: 'Exactly!', 'Right!'
concepts.explanation: In conversation, Germans say Genau! very often to agree with someone or confirm what they said, much like 'Exactly!' or 'Right!'. It can stand alone or start a sentence: Genau, so ist es.

concepts.title: wenig vs. ein wenig
concepts.explanation: wenig means 'little, not much' and sounds negative: Ich habe wenig Zeit = I don't have much time. With ein in front, ein wenig means 'a little, some' and sounds positive: ein wenig Englisch = a little English. Before a noun, wenig usually takes no ending.

concepts.title: ein bisschen: 'a bit'
concepts.explanation: ein bisschen means 'a bit, a little' and is the everyday word for it (ein wenig sounds a bit more formal). It never changes its form: ein bisschen Kaffee, ein bisschen spät. kein bisschen means 'not one bit, not at all'.

examples.text: Das ist ein bisschen zu viel.
Das hat mir kein bisschen gefallen.
examples.en: I didn't like that one bit.

concepts.title: fertig mit: 'done with'
concepts.explanation: To say you're done with something, use fertig sein mit + dative. The thing you've finished comes after mit, and fertig usually goes at the end: Ich bin mit der Arbeit fertig = I'm done with work. Without mit, Ich bin fertig just means 'I'm done' or 'I'm ready'.

examples.text: Bist du mit dem Buch fertig?
examples.en: Are you done with the book?

examples.text: Er ist mit der Schule fertig.
Ich bin mit der Arbeit fertig.

concepts.title: kaum: 'hardly', 'hardly any'
concepts.explanation: kaum means 'hardly' or 'barely'. Before a noun it means 'hardly any', and you don't add kein: Ich habe kaum Zeit = I hardly have any time. kaum etwas = hardly anything, kaum jemand = hardly anyone.

concepts.title: sein + participle: a finished state
concepts.explanation: sein + past participle describes a state, the result of something done: Das Buch ist auf Englisch geschrieben = The book is written in English. Compare werden + participle, which describes the action happening: Das wird geschrieben = It is being written.

examples.text: Das Buch ist auf Englisch geschrieben.
examples.en: The book is written in English.

concepts.title: kennen vs. wissen: two verbs for 'know'
concepts.explanation: kennen means knowing a person, place or thing because you're familiar with it: Er kennt mich = He knows me. wissen means knowing a fact or information, often followed by dass, wo, was, etc.: Er weiß, wo das Haus ist. kennen takes a direct object; you can't use wissen with a person.

examples.text: Sie kennt die Stadt, aber sie weiß nicht, wo das Haus ist.
examples.en: She knows the city, but she doesn't know where the house is.

concepts.title: Sag mal, ...: 'tell me', 'say'
concepts.explanation: Sag mal at the start of a question is a casual way to get someone's attention or bring up a new topic, like English 'say, ...' or 'tell me, ...'. It's informal, used with people you call du: Sag mal, hast du heute Zeit?

examples.text: Sag mal, hast du heute Zeit?
examples.en: Say, do you have time today?

examples.text: Sag mal, wo ist mein Buch?
Sag mal, wie spät ist es?

concepts.title: eigentlich: 'actually' and 'by the way'
concepts.explanation: In statements, eigentlich means 'actually, in fact, really', often hinting that reality is a bit different: Eigentlich habe ich keine Zeit ('Actually, I don't have time'). In questions it softens and adds interest, like 'by the way' or 'anyway': Wie heißt du eigentlich? It's very common in everyday speech.

examples.en: What's your name, by the way?

concepts.title: bevor: 'before' (verb at the end)
concepts.explanation: bevor joins a whole clause and means 'before'. Like dass and weil, it sends the verb to the end: bevor es zu spät ist ('before it's too late'). Don't confuse it with vor, which goes before a noun: vor dem Essen.

examples.text: Ich muss gehen, bevor es zu spät ist.
examples.en: I have to go before it's too late.

examples.text: Bevor er kam, war alles gut.
examples.en: Before he came, everything was fine.

examples.text: Das war, bevor wir Kinder hatten.
examples.en: That was before we had kids.

concepts.title: The -en ending on adjectives
concepts.explanation: -en is the most common adjective ending. You use it after den and einen (masculine objects), after dem, einem and einer (dative), and in the plural after die, keine or meine: einen großen Hund, in einem großen Haus, die großen Kinder. If in doubt in these spots, -en is usually right.

examples.text: Sie leben in einem großen Haus.
examples.en: They live in a big house.

examples.text: Die großen Kinder gehen schon zur Schule.
examples.en: The older children already go to school.

concepts.title: beide: 'both'
concepts.explanation: beide means 'both'. It can stand before a plural noun (beide Kinder = both children) or on its own (Beide sind hier = Both are here). With a pronoun subject it usually comes after the verb: Wir haben beide Angst = We're both afraid.

examples.text: Beide Kinder sind in der Schule.

concepts.title: hin: movement 'to there'
concepts.explanation: German separates where something is (wo) from where something goes. hin marks movement away from the speaker, and in questions it often splits from wo and goes to the end: Wo willst du hin? = Where do you want to go? You can also say da hin = (to) there.

examples.en: Where do you want to go?
I don't want to go there.

concepts.title: halten von: 'to think of'
concepts.explanation: halten von is used to ask for or give an opinion: Was halten Sie davon? = What do you think of it? Something you don't rate highly: nicht viel von ... halten = not think much of.

examples.en: What do you think of it?
What do you think of him?

examples.text: Sie halten nicht viel von mir.
examples.en: They don't think much of me.

concepts.title: halten für: 'to consider, take for'
concepts.explanation: halten + accusative + für means 'to consider something (to be) ...' or 'to take someone for ...': Wir halten das für richtig = We think that's right. It's also how you say someone mistakes you for another person.

examples.text: Viele Menschen halten das für wahr.
Sie halten mich für einen anderen.
examples.en: They're mistaking me for someone else.

concepts.title: danke and bitte
concepts.explanation: Danke means 'thanks'; Danke schön or Danke sehr is stronger. The usual reply is Bitte ('you're welcome'). Nein, danke politely declines, and danke für + accusative says what you're thankful for: Danke für alles.

concepts.title: danken takes the dative
concepts.explanation: The verb danken ('to thank') takes the dative, like helfen: Ich danke dir (not dich). The thing you're thanking for comes with für.

examples.text: Ich danke Ihnen für Ihre Hilfe.

examples.en: I thank you all for everything.

concepts.title: morgen früh: 'tomorrow morning'
concepts.explanation: früh means 'early', but after morgen or heute it means 'in the morning': morgen früh = tomorrow morning, heute früh = this morning. Note: morgen früh, never 'morgen Morgen'.

examples.text: Ich habe ihn heute früh gesehen.

concepts.title: zum ersten Mal: 'for the first time'
concepts.explanation: erst- means 'first' and takes adjective endings like any adjective: am ersten Tag, die ersten Tage. 'For the first time' is zum ersten Mal (zum = zu dem).

examples.text: Ich bin zum ersten Mal in Berlin.
examples.en: I'm in Berlin for the first time.

examples.text: Am ersten Tag war ich allein.
examples.en: On the first day I was alone.
The first few days were hard.

concepts.title: ist geworden: the perfect of werden
concepts.explanation: werden ('to become') forms its perfect with sein: Es ist spät geworden = It has gotten late. Was ist aus ihm geworden? asks 'What became of him?'. In the passive the participle shortens to worden: Es ist gemacht worden.

concepts.title: lässt sich: 'can be done'
concepts.explanation: es lässt sich + infinitive means that something can be done. It's a common way to say 'it's possible' without naming who does it. Das lässt sich machen = 'That can be done.'

concepts.title: weiter + verb: 'keep doing, go on'
concepts.explanation: Put weiter with a verb to say someone continues doing it. In the sentence, weiter goes to the end like a separable particle. Sie spricht weiter = 'She keeps talking.' Wie geht es weiter? = 'What happens next?'

concepts.title: Das ist mir wichtig: 'it matters to me'
concepts.explanation: To say something is important to someone, German often uses the dative pronoun without a preposition: mir, dir, ihm. Das ist mir wichtig = 'That's important to me.' You can also say für mich, but the dative is very common.

examples.text: Meine Familie ist mir sehr wichtig.
examples.en: My family is very important to me.

concepts.title: Verbs as nouns: das Essen
concepts.explanation: Any German verb can become a noun: just capitalize the infinitive and use das. essen (to eat) becomes das Essen (food, the meal), leben becomes das Leben (life). These nouns are always neuter.

concepts.title: sonst: 'otherwise' and 'else'
concepts.explanation: sonst means 'otherwise, or else': Wir müssen gehen, sonst kommen wir zu spät. It counts as the first element of its clause, so the verb comes right after it (sonst kommen wir). With question words it means 'else': Was sonst? (What else?)

examples.text: Wir müssen gehen, sonst kommen wir zu spät.
examples.en: We have to go, otherwise we'll be late.

concepts.title: nun mal: 'that's just how it is'
concepts.explanation: nun mal (or just mal) adds the feeling 'that's simply the way it is, nothing can change it'. Das ist nun mal so means 'That's just the way it is.' It often sounds a little resigned or like a shrug.

examples.en: That's just the way it is.

examples.text: Ich bin nun mal kein Lehrer.
Er ist nun mal mein Bruder.

concepts.title: so weit sein: 'to be ready'
concepts.explanation: weit means 'far', but so weit sein means 'to be ready' or 'to have reached that point'. Bist du so weit? is 'Are you ready?', and Es ist so weit means 'The time has come.'

examples.en: I'll be ready in a moment.

concepts.title: Guten Morgen, Guten Tag, Guten Abend
concepts.explanation: These greetings are short for 'I wish you a good day', so gut takes the -en ending of a masculine object: Guten Tag! Morgen, Tag and Abend are all masculine. Nacht is feminine, so it's Gute Nacht.

examples.text: Guten Abend, wie geht es Ihnen?

concepts.title: auf dem Tisch vs. auf den Tisch: location or direction
concepts.explanation: Some prepositions (auf, in, an, unter, vor, über, zwischen) take the dative when they say where something is, and the accusative when they say where something is going. Ask 'where?' (dative): Das Buch liegt auf dem Tisch. Ask 'where to?' (accusative): Kommt an den Tisch!

examples.text: Das Buch liegt auf dem Tisch.
examples.en: The book is on the table.

examples.text: Die Katze ist unter dem Tisch.
examples.en: The cat is under the table.

concepts.title: zum Arzt, beim Arzt: going to vs. being at
concepts.explanation: To go to a person or their practice or home, German uses zu: Ich gehe zum Arzt ('to the doctor's'). Once you are there, you use bei: Ich bin beim Arzt ('at the doctor's'). Both take the dative.

examples.en: I have to go to the doctor.
I was at the doctor's yesterday.
You should go to the doctor.

concepts.title: ein guter Mann: the -er ending after ein
concepts.explanation: After der, an adjective just ends in -e: der gute Mann. But ein, kein and mein have no ending in the masculine nominative, so the adjective shows the gender instead with -er: ein guter Mann, kein guter Tag. With no article at all you also get -er: Guter Hund!

concepts.title: die beiden: 'the two (of them)'
concepts.explanation: beide alone means 'both', but with an article or possessive it becomes beiden: die beiden = 'the two of them', meine beiden Kinder = 'both my children'. Die beiden can stand on its own for two people: Ich kenne die beiden ('I know those two').

examples.en: The two of them are friends.
I know the two of them.

concepts.title: euer / eure: 'your' for several people
concepts.explanation: When you say 'your' to several people you call ihr, use euer. It takes the same endings as mein, and the e before r drops when an ending is added: euer Hund, but eure Katze, eure Eltern.

concepts.title: -in: the female form of a noun
concepts.explanation: Adding -in to a masculine noun for a person makes the female version, and it is always feminine (die): der Freund becomes die Freundin, der Lehrer becomes die Lehrerin. Some also get an umlaut: der Arzt, die Ärztin.

examples.text: Marika ist eine Freundin von mir.
examples.en: Marika is a friend of mine.
